Subword Tokenization.module_md:
## Module Overview
Imagine you are building a multilingual language model for search and keep encountering many rare words, misspellings, and new product names that your vocabulary treats as unknown. Subword tokenization solves this by breaking words into reusable parts so unseen words still get meaningful representations. This topic matters now because industry-scale pretraining and production NLP systems rely on robust, compact vocabularies (BPE/WordPiece-style) but increasingly require probabilistic and byte-level alternatives, evaluation practices, and tokenizer engineering to scale reliably. In this module you will move beyond the course’s BPE/WordPiece foundations to learn the probabilistic Unigram approach (SentencePiece-style), practical tokenizer training and evaluation, and how these choices affect pretraining and production. Ready to see how a tokenizer can change model performance and costs in real systems?

## Learning Objectives
1. Explain the Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) merge process and how WordPiece-style subword splitting mitigates UNK tokens. (Curriculum)  
2. Implement a subword tokenizer training pipeline: prepare corpus, choose model type, train vocabulary, and save model artifacts. (Gap — Apply)  
3. Compare the greedy BPE merge approach to the Unigram (SentencePiece) probabilistic model and evaluate their trade-offs for pretraining. (Gap — Analyze)  
4. Evaluate tokenizer quality using measurable metrics (OOV/coverage, average tokens-per-word, fragmentation) and decide a vocab size for a given corpus. (Gap — Evaluate)  
5. Apply stochastic tokenization (e.g., subword sampling / BPE-dropout) during pretraining to increase robustness; justify the choice with experimental diagnostics. (Gap — Apply)

## Curriculum Coverage
The course teaches subword modeling as a way to reason about structure below the word level (parts of words, characters, bytes). It presents the dominant modern paradigm: learning a vocabulary of parts of words so that at training and testing time each word is split into a sequence of known subwords. The byte-pair encoding algorithm is explained step-by-step: start with characters plus an end-of-word symbol, find the most common adjacent character pair in a corpus, add that pair as a subword, replace occurrences, and repeat until the desired vocabulary size is reached. The curriculum notes that BPE was originally used in machine translation and that similar methods (WordPiece) are used in pretrained models.

Course materials illustrate how common words end up as single subword tokens while rarer or novel words are split into multiple pieces (sometimes intuitive, sometimes not). Examples show how misspellings, morphological variants, and novel items are represented as sequences of subwords, and the curriculum explains UNK mitigation by splitting unknown words into subwords so even unseen words get representations. Practical emphasis in the course is on understanding the algorithmic steps, seeing examples of mappings from words to subwords, and recognizing why distributional representations built over subwords improve similarity handling over one-hot word symbols.

Before continuing, make sure you can answer:
- What are the basic iterative steps of the byte-pair encoding algorithm?
- How does splitting into subword tokens mitigate the UNK problem?
- What role do common vs. rare words play in the learned subword vocabulary?

## Identified Gaps
The curriculum gives a solid grounding in BPE and WordPiece and the motivation for subword vocabularies, but industry practice expects additional capabilities that the course treats lightly or omits. These gaps are opportunities to build practical, employable skills.

- Missing probabilistic tokenization (Unigram / SentencePiece): The course does not cover Unigram Language Model tokenization, a widely used alternative that treats tokenization probabilistically rather than via greedy merges. Why it matters: many production/pretraining pipelines prefer this approach for better tokenization quality and for enabling subword regularization. Priority: (Critical).
- Practical tokenizer engineering and evaluation: The curriculum lacks hands-on guidance on normalization, Unicode handling, pre-tokenization rules, vocab-size selection, and diagnostic metrics (OOV, tokens-per-sentence, fragmentation). Why it matters: employers expect reproducible, well-evaluated tokenizers tailored to domain or multilingual corpora. Priority: (Critical).
- Byte-level and multilingual strategies, stochastic tokenization (BPE-dropout/subword sampling), and tooling concerns (model serialization, fast tokenizers) are also undercovered but can be learned incrementally. These are Important for robustness and scalability in industry. Priority: (Important).

## Core Content
This section teaches the missing, industry-relevant material: probabilistic Unigram tokenization and practical tokenizer engineering & evaluation.

### What You Need to Learn

Building on the BPE and WordPiece concepts you studied, learn the Unigram (SentencePiece) approach:
- Definition and motivation:
  - The Unigram model learns a probabilistic inventory of candidate subword pieces and treats tokenization as finding the highest-likelihood segmentation of a word under that inventory. Unlike greedy merges driven by frequency, Unigram scores alternative segmentations probabilistically and can support sampling multiple segmentations for the same input.
- How it works (walkthrough and example):
  - High-level process: initialize a large candidate vocabulary (often via substrings), assign probabilities to candidates, optimize those probabilities to maximize corpus likelihood (pruning low-probability pieces), and output a compact vocabulary whose pieces explain the corpus well.
  - Concrete example: suppose candidates include "re", "act", "react", "ion", "react##ion". The model assigns probabilities and chooses segmentations; if "react" has high probability, words like "reactivate" may prefer "react" + "ivate" segmentation, whereas rare splits remain possible.
- How to apply (step-by-step):
  1. Prepare a normalized corpus (Unicode-normalized, consistent casing policy) and remove unwanted markup.
  2. Choose SentencePiece "unigram" model type and set a target vocab size (iterate if needed).
  3. Train the model: the trainer optimizes piece probabilities and prunes low-score candidates until the target vocab is reached.
  4. Validate by inspecting tokenization of held-out lines and measuring metrics (coverage, avg tokens per word).
  5. Optionally enable subword regularization / sampling during pretraining to randomly sample alternative tokenizations per input (improves robustness).
- Industry example:
  - Companies training large multilingual models use SentencePiece Unigram to obtain a compact, language-agnostic vocabulary and to enable subword sampling during pretraining so the model sees multiple plausible segmentations of morphologically rich words. This helps generalize to rare forms and reduces overfitting to a single segmentation.

Practical tokenizer engineering and evaluation (what industry expects):
- Definition and scope:
  - Tokenizer engineering covers corpus normalization/Unicode handling, pre-tokenization choices (whitespace vs. character splitting), vocabulary-size selection, special-token policies, serialization of models and merges, and performance considerations (speed, memory).
- Detailed walkthrough and example:
  - Why normalization matters: inconsistent Unicode or casing produces noisy candidate statistics; normalize (e.g., Unicode NFC/NFKC) and decide a casing policy (lowercase vs. case-preserving with case embeddings).
  - Choosing vocab size and evaluating trade-offs: larger vocab reduces tokens-per-word and may lower sequence length (saving compute per pass), but increases embedding-table size (memory/cost). Use measurable diagnostics: OOV/coverage (fraction of characters/words not covered), average tokens-per-sentence, and fragmentation rate (how often words split into many pieces).
- How to apply (step-by-step):
  1. Collect representatively sampled corpus appropriate to the downstream task(s) or pretraining mix (include domain/multilingual balance if needed).
  2. Normalize text consistently (Unicode normalization, optional lowercasing or preserve-case rules).
  3. Pre-tokenize if useful (e.g., split on whitespace for languages with spaces; for scripts without spaces use character-based preprocessing).
  4. Train candidate tokenizer(s) (BPE and/or Unigram) at several vocab sizes.
  5. Compute diagnostics on a validation set: tokens-per-word, tokens-per-sentence, coverage and frequency distribution of pieces.
  6. Inspect failure cases (long fragmentations, frequent rare tokens) and iterate (adjust vocab size, add normalization rules, or switch to byte-level if many unseen codepoints).
- Industry example:
  - A search/product company trains tokenizers on mixed-language logs. They detect high fragmentation for named entities and adjust normalization and vocab size, leading to fewer tokens per query and reduced latency in production. They also save tokenizer model artifacts and version them for reproducibility.

Brief summaries of remaining gaps
- Byte-level tokenization: a byte-level vocabulary maps raw bytes (eliminating UNK) and simplifies multilingual coverage; it trades longer sequences for simpler OOV handling. Why it matters: deterministic round-trip and no UNK. Where to learn more: SentencePiece docs and comparative evaluation papers.
- Stochastic tokenization (BPE-dropout / subword regularization): sampling tokenizations during training reduces overfitting to one segmentation and improves robustness. Why it matters: better generalization during pretraining. Where to learn more: Subword Regularization paper (see Further Reading).

### Common Misconceptions
- Misconception: "Unigram and BPE are the same except for implementation details."  
  - Why it’s wrong: BPE is a greedy, frequency-driven merge process producing deterministic merges; Unigram is a probabilistic inventory that scores and selects segmentations based on likelihood, enabling sampling and different trade-offs.  
  - Correct understanding: They are different modeling paradigms with distinct optimization criteria and implications for tokenization variability and robustness.
- Misconception: "If you use subword tokenization you never need to worry about OOV or UNK."  
  - Why it’s wrong: Some tokenizers (character-level or byte-level) can eliminate UNK, but BPE/WordPiece with limited vocabularies can still produce very long fragmentations or rare pieces that hurt efficiency. Practical engineering (vocab size, normalization) is needed to minimize negative effects.  
  - Correct understanding: Subword models mitigate UNK but do not automatically solve fragmentation, efficiency, or multilingual distribution issues.
- Misconception: "Deterministic segmentation is always better for model quality."  
  - Why it’s wrong: Deterministic segmentation can cause the model to overfit to a single decomposition; stochastic tokenization during pretraining often improves robustness.  
  - Correct understanding: Deterministic tokenization is simpler and reproducible, but stochastic methods can improve generalization and should be considered during pretraining experiments.

## Industry Context
Subword tokenization skills are valued in roles such as:
- NLP Engineer / Applied NLP Scientist
- Machine Learning Engineer specializing in pretraining pipelines
- Research Engineer working on tokenization and data pipelines for large language models

Real-world use case (detailed): A multinational e-commerce company must index product titles in dozens of languages, many of which contain brand names, product codes, and misspellings. They train a Unigram (SentencePiece) tokenizer on a mixed-language corpus with byte-level fallbacks and enable subword sampling during model pretraining. Outcome: improved handling of rare brand tokens, reduced rate of pathological fragmentations for non-Latin scripts, and better retrieval quality across languages. They also evaluate tokenizer choices with tokens-per-query and embedding-table cost metrics to balance latency and memory in production.

When hiring for these roles, employers look for:
- Practical experience training and validating tokenizers on real corpora, including normalization and multilingual balancing.
- Ability to measure tokenizer diagnostics (coverage, fragmentation, tokens-per-sentence) and to justify vocab-size decisions relative to computational constraints.
- Familiarity with probabilistic tokenizers (Unigram/SentencePiece), stochastic tokenization techniques, and saving/versioning tokenizer artifacts for reproducible pretraining.

## Practice & Review

### Quick Check
1. What are the iterative steps of byte-pair encoding?  
> Answer: Start with characters plus an end-of-word symbol; find the most common adjacent character pair in the corpus; add that pair to the vocabulary; replace occurrences; repeat until reaching target vocab size.

2. How does subword splitting mitigate the UNK problem?  
> Answer: By splitting unknown words into known subword pieces (characters or learned subwords), models can produce embeddings for rare or unseen words instead of mapping them to a single UNK token.

3. Conceptual: In one sentence, how does a Unigram (SentencePiece) model differ from greedy BPE?  
> Answer: Unigram learns a probabilistic inventory and scores possible segmentations to maximize corpus likelihood (allowing sampling), whereas BPE greedily merges frequent adjacent symbols into deterministic merges.

4. Application: You trained a BPE tokenizer and see many long fragmentations for names in a domain corpus. What sequence of actions combines course knowledge and core content to address this?  
> Answer: Normalize the corpus (Unicode/casing), consider increasing vocab size or adding domain-specific tokens, retrain using Unigram or byte-level fallback, and evaluate fragmentation and tokens-per-sentence metrics to choose the best configuration.

### Apply It
Scenario: You are given a 10-million-line multilingual product title corpus for pretraining a domain-adapted language model. The initial BPE tokenizer produces many fragmented tokens for non-Latin scripts and product codes, increasing sequence lengths and training cost.

Tasks:
- Train a Unigram (SentencePiece) tokenizer on the corpus and save model artifacts and vocab.
- Compute diagnostics on a held-out validation set: average tokens-per-sentence, fragmentation rate for named entities, and vocabulary coverage.
- Experiment with one of: (a) byte-level fallback, (b) adding frequent product-code tokens to the training data, or (c) increasing vocab size; compare diagnostics.
- If pretraining, enable subword sampling for one experiment and measure validation perplexity difference (or a proxy downstream metric).

Expected deliverable: A short report (2–3 pages) including tokenizer model files, a table of diagnostic metrics for each experiment, example tokenizations of failure cases, and a recommended tokenizer configuration with justification.

## Key Takeaways
- Curriculum: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) iteratively merges the most frequent adjacent character pairs into subword units until a target vocabulary size is reached.
- Curriculum: WordPiece-style and other subword tokenizers map rare or novel words into sequences of learned subwords so models can represent unseen words without an UNK embedding.
- Curriculum: Subword modeling reduces vocabulary size and helps models generalize to misspellings, morphological variants, and novel items by composing representations from parts.
- Gap: Unigram (SentencePiece) is a probabilistic alternative to greedy BPE that optimizes a likelihood-based inventory and enables subword sampling for robustness.
- Gap: Practical tokenizer engineering (normalization, pre-tokenization, vocab-size selection, diagnostics like tokens-per-sentence and fragmentation) is essential for production and pretraining efficiency.
- Gap: Byte-level tokenization and stochastic tokenization (BPE-dropout / subword regularization) are important tools to eliminate UNK and improve generalization, respectively.
- Integration: Choose a tokenization method (BPE, WordPiece, Unigram, byte-level) based on corpus characteristics; combine this choice with careful normalization and diagnostics to balance model quality and computational cost.
- Integration: During pretraining, consider stochastic tokenization or sampling to increase robustness; during production, prioritize deterministic, reproducible tokenizer artifacts and versioning.

## Reflection
- What was the most important thing you learned in this module?
- Which gap area do you feel least confident about? What would help you strengthen it?
- How does Subword Tokenization connect to other topics you have studied?

## Further Reading
- [SentencePiece: A simple and language independent subword tokenizer and detokenizer](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.06226) (Research Paper) — (Intermediate) — Learn the Unigram model approach and practical tooling for language-independent tokenization.  
- [Subword Regularization: Improving Neural Network Translation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.10959) (Research Paper) — (Advanced) — Introduces subword sampling and regularization methods (BPE-dropout / subword regularization) to improve robustness.  
- [Hugging Face: Tokenizers documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/tokenizers) (Documentation) — (Beginner) — Practical APIs and guidance for training, serializing, and evaluating tokenizers used in industry workflows.  
- [Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units (BPE introduction)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.07909) (Research Paper) — (Intermediate) — The original practical introduction of BPE for machine translation and handling rare words.  
- [Recent evaluation work on subword tokenization (examples of comparative studies)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.06663) (Research Paper) — (Advanced) — Comparative analyses and evaluation approaches for modern subword tokenization choices.

Encoder-Only Pretraining.module_md:
## Module Overview
Imagine you are building a question-answering system for customer support and you need sentence- and span-level representations that capture context from both left and right of each token. Encoder-only pretraining (BERT, RoBERTa, SpanBERT) solves this by producing bidirectional contextual embeddings that transfer well to classification, tagging, and span-extraction tasks. Right now industry still trains and deploys encoder models widely for NLU tasks, but employers also expect knowledge of more compute- and sample-efficient pretraining objectives and practical pretraining recipes. This module teaches the curriculum’s core MLM-based encoder pretraining and, critically, fills the industry gaps: replaced-token-detection (ELECTRA-style) and advanced masking/span strategies (dynamic masking, whole-word/span masking), plus how they affect downstream transfer. Ready to learn how to pretrain encoders that are faster to train and better for span tasks?

## Learning Objectives
1. Explain the Masked Language Modeling (MLM) objective and the role of encoder-only architectures such as BERT, RoBERTa, and SpanBERT. (Curriculum)  
2. Describe how span masking (SpanBERT) and whole-word masking modify the MLM task to improve span-level representations. (Curriculum)  
3. Compare and contrast MLM with replaced-token-detection (ELECTRA-style), evaluating their trade-offs in sample and compute efficiency. (Gap)  
4. Implement a basic replaced-token-detection pretraining pipeline: train a small generator, create replaced-token inputs, and train the discriminator encoder. (Gap — Apply)  
5. Analyze and design a pretraining recipe that chooses masking strategy and pretraining objective for a specific downstream task (e.g., NER vs. sentence classification). (Gap — Analyze/Evaluate)

## Curriculum Coverage
The course teaches encoder-only pretraining by motivating encoders as models that capture bidirectional context — they can condition on both left and right contexts, which is useful for many understanding tasks. Because standard causal language modeling (used by decoder models) cannot condition on future tokens, encoders instead use a denoising-style objective: Masked Language Modeling (MLM). In MLM, a fraction of tokens in each input are replaced with a special [MASK] token, and the encoder is trained to predict those masked tokens; only masked positions contribute to the loss. This gives rise to powerful token and sentence representations usable for downstream fine-tuning.

The curriculum also presents several practical encoder families and extensions: BERT as the canonical MLM-pretrained encoder; RoBERTa as an improved recipe that trains longer and removes Next Sentence Prediction; and SpanBERT which masks contiguous spans of tokens to produce stronger span-level representations. The materials emphasize fine-tuning workflows (taking pretrained encoder representations and training downstream classifiers or span-extraction heads) and discuss limitations of encoders for generation tasks.

Before continuing, make sure you can answer:
- What is the core supervised signal used during encoder-only pretraining?  
- Why do encoders use a masked/denoising objective instead of standard autoregressive language modeling?  
- What modification does SpanBERT introduce to the basic MLM setup?

## Identified Gaps
The curriculum provides a strong conceptual foundation in MLM and encoder variants, and now you can build on that to match industry expectations. However, there are several clear opportunities to add practical, industry-relevant skills:

- Alternative encoder pretraining objectives (Missing): The curriculum does not cover replaced-token-detection (ELECTRA) — a discriminator-based objective that often yields equal or better downstream performance while using less compute and data. Why it matters: employers value compute- and sample-efficient pretraining methods for practical model development. Priority: (Critical).

- Masking and span strategies in the pretraining recipe (Underdeveloped): The curriculum mentions span masking (SpanBERT) and RoBERTa improvements but does not fully explore dynamic masking, whole-word masking, span-boundary objectives, or how masking hyperparameters affect downstream transfer. Why it matters: masking design materially affects representations for NER, coreference, and other span tasks. Priority: (Critical).

- Pretraining engineering and data practices (Underdeveloped): Practical skills such as data deduplication, mixed-precision training, optimizer choices for large-batch runs, and domain-adaptive continued pretraining are only lightly covered. Why it matters: running robust pretraining pipelines is essential for reproducible results and deployment. Priority: (Important).

- Parameter-efficient fine-tuning and evaluation practices (Underdeveloped): The curriculum doesn’t cover adapters/LoRA and systematic transfer evaluation. Why it matters: production teams often rely on parameter-efficient adaptation and standardized downstream evaluation. Priority: (Important).

Each gap is therefore an opportunity: learning these will increase your employability and make your pretraining and fine-tuning more effective in real projects.

## Core Content

### What You Need to Learn

Gap 1 — Replaced-Token Detection (ELECTRA-style) (Critical)  
Building on your understanding of MLM (predicting masked tokens from bidirectional context), replaced-token-detection reframes encoder pretraining as a discriminative task: detect which tokens in the input have been replaced by plausible alternatives. Definition: replaced-token-detection trains an encoder (the discriminator) to perform a binary classification per token — was this token replaced by a generator or is it the original? Practically, training uses a small generative model (generator) to propose token replacements; the discriminator sees the sequence with replacements and learns to label each token as original vs. replaced.

How it works — walkthrough:
1. Train or use a small generator (often an MLM-style model) to predict token candidates for masked positions given context.  
2. Use the generator to replace masked tokens in the original text with sampled token predictions, producing a corrupted input where some tokens are original and others are replaced.  
3. Train the discriminator encoder on this corrupted input, with a binary cross-entropy loss at each token: predict 1 if token is original, 0 if replaced.  
4. After pretraining, discard the generator and use the discriminator’s encoder weights for downstream fine-tuning.

Step-by-step implementation (practical recipe):
1. Prepare pretraining corpus and tokenizer (you already know how to tokenize for MLM).  
2. Initialize a small generator (e.g., smaller Transformer) and a larger discriminator (encoder).  
3. For each batch: sample masking positions, run generator to produce replacement tokens, construct corrupted input, compute discriminator token-level replaced/not-replaced targets, update generator (optional, via MLM loss) and discriminator (primary).  
4. Periodically evaluate the discriminator’s representations by fine-tuning on downstream tasks or monitoring proxy metrics.  
5. Save checkpoints and, for deployment, use discriminator weights as the pretrained encoder.

Industry example: teams seeking faster pretraining runs use ELECTRA-style objectives to get comparable or better downstream transfer using fewer compute-hours and less data; the generator/discriminator setup is an engineering pattern you can adopt when compute is constrained.

Gap 2 — Masking Strategies: Dynamic Masking, Whole-Word Masking, and Span Masking (Critical)  
Building on MLM and SpanBERT’s contiguous-span masking, masking strategy choices determine what distribution of prediction problems the encoder sees and therefore what kinds of representations it learns. Definitions:
- Dynamic masking: regenerate masks on the fly each time a sequence is sampled, so the model sees different masked tokens across epochs.  
- Whole-word masking: when a subword from a word is masked, mask all its subword pieces together so the model must predict the entire word.  
- Span masking (SpanBERT-style): mask contiguous spans of tokens rather than independently masking tokens, and optionally use span-boundary objectives that force the model to better represent span endpoints and internal structure.

How it works — walkthrough and why it helps:
1. Dynamic masking: each training step samples new mask positions for tokens; this increases the effective number of prediction contexts the model experiences and reduces overfitting to a single static mask pattern.  
2. Whole-word masking: mitigates subword fragmentation effects by presenting the model with the full lexical item to predict, which is especially helpful when many tokens are subword pieces.  
3. Span masking and span-boundary objective: by removing contiguous spans, the model is forced to reason about multi-token units and their boundaries — useful for tasks that require span-level representations (NER, coreference, QA).

Step-by-step for applying span masking (practical recipe):
1. Choose a masking budget (e.g., fraction of tokens to mask per sequence) and a span-length distribution (e.g., geometric or fixed-length).  
2. For each sequence, sample span start positions and span lengths until the masking budget is filled.  
3. Replace spans with [MASK] tokens or special placeholders, or follow SpanBERT’s span-boundary objective which focuses on predicting span representations/boundaries instead of only token identities.  
4. Use dynamic masking so spans differ each epoch; experiment with whole-word alignment when tokenizer produces subwords.

Industry example: projects focused on NER, span extraction, or coreference often prefer span masking or SpanBERT-style objectives because they directly improve the model’s learning signal for contiguous text units.

Brief summaries of other gaps (where to learn more):
- Pretraining engineering and data practices: data deduplication, mixed-precision, and large-batch optimizers (e.g., LAMB) materially affect cost and stability — learn from The Pile and optimizer literature.  
- Parameter-efficient fine-tuning: adapters and low-rank updates (LoRA) let you adapt large encoder weights with fewer trainable parameters — see adapter and LoRA papers for implementation patterns.

### Common Misconceptions
- Misconception: "MLM is always the best objective for encoder pretraining."  
  Why it’s wrong: alternatives like replaced-token-detection can match or surpass MLM performance while using less compute and data. Correct view: MLM is effective and conceptually simple, but objective choice should consider compute budget and downstream tasks.

- Misconception: "Masking choice is a minor tuning detail."  
  Why it’s wrong: masking design (dynamic vs static, span vs token, whole-word) changes what prediction problems the model sees and thus the representations it learns, particularly for span-centric tasks. Correct view: treat masking strategy as a core part of the pretraining recipe to tune for your target tasks.

- Misconception: "If I use span masking, I don't need to adjust downstream fine-tuning."  
  Why it’s wrong: better span representations may reduce but not eliminate the need to design task-specific heads (e.g., span boundary classifiers or answer span scorers). Correct view: align pretraining signals with downstream architecture and objective design.

## Industry Context
Roles that value encoder-only pretraining skills include: NLP Research Engineer, Applied NLP Scientist, and ML Engineer (NLP-focused). These roles often require the ability to design pretraining objectives, run scalable pretraining experiments, and fine-tune encoders for production tasks.

Real-world use case (detailed): A legal-tech company needs high-quality named entity recognition and span extraction from long contracts. They perform domain-adaptive pretraining by continuing encoder pretraining on a curated corpus of legal text, using span masking to emphasize contiguous legal entities and whole-word masking to avoid subword fragmentation. To reduce cost, they evaluate an ELECTRA-style objective so pretraining converges with fewer compute hours. Outcome: improved NER/F1 and faster iteration on model variants during development, enabling more reliable extraction pipelines for downstream contract-analysis tools.

Employers hiring for these roles look for: familiarity with encoder pretraining objectives (MLM and alternatives), experience selecting masking strategies for specific tasks, ability to run reproducible pretraining jobs (checkpointing, mixed precision), and knowledge of fine-tuning or parameter-efficient adaptation techniques to deploy models efficiently.

## Practice & Review

### Quick Check
1. What is the training signal used in Masked Language Modeling (MLM)?  
> Answer: Predict the identity of tokens that have been replaced by [MASK] in the input; loss is computed only on masked positions.

2. Name two encoder-family variants mentioned in the curriculum and one distinguishing change for each.  
> Answer: RoBERTa — trains longer and removes Next Sentence Prediction; SpanBERT — masks contiguous spans of tokens to improve span representations.

3. Conceptual: What are the two main components in an ELECTRA-style replaced-token-detection pretraining setup, and what does each do?  
> Answer: Generator — a smaller model that proposes plausible token replacements for masked positions; Discriminator — the encoder trained to classify each token as original or replaced.

4. Application: If your downstream task is coreference resolution, which masking strategy should you consider and why?  
> Answer: Span masking or span-boundary objectives, because they encourage learning contiguous span representations and boundaries that coreference resolution depends on.

### Apply It
Scenario: You are asked to pretrain an encoder to improve a biomedical NER system. You have limited compute and a mid-sized in-domain corpus. Use your curriculum knowledge of MLM and SpanBERT plus gap knowledge about ELECTRA and masking strategies to design a pretraining plan.

Tasks:
- Decide whether to use MLM, ELECTRA-style replaced-token-detection, or a hybrid; justify based on compute/data constraints.  
- Choose a masking strategy (dynamic/static, whole-word or span masking) and specify sampling steps for spans.  
- Sketch a high-level training loop: generator/discriminator steps (if using ELECTRA), checkpoint schedule, and downstream evaluation plan on a validation NER set.  
- Produce a short report summarizing expected trade-offs and next experiments to run.

Expected deliverable: a 1–2 page pretraining plan that lists the objective chosen, masking algorithm and hyperparameters, training workflow (including how generator and discriminator interact if used), and a validation protocol describing metrics and checkpoints.

## Key Takeaways
- Curriculum: Encoder-only pretraining uses a denoising-style objective (MLM) so models can leverage bidirectional context.  
- Curriculum: BERT, RoBERTa, and SpanBERT are major encoder families; RoBERTa refines the pretraining recipe, SpanBERT masks spans to strengthen span representations.  
- Curriculum: Pretrained encoder weights are typically fine-tuned for downstream classification, tagging, and span-extraction tasks.

- Gap: Replaced-token-detection (ELECTRA-style) is an efficient alternative to MLM that trains a discriminator to detect replaced tokens and can yield similar or better transfer with less compute.  
- Gap: Masking strategy (dynamic masking, whole-word masking, span masking, span-boundary objectives) strongly influences downstream performance for span-centric tasks.  
- Gap: Practical pretraining engineering (data deduplication, mixed precision, optimizer choices like LAMB) and domain-adaptive continued pretraining are important for real-world success.

- Integration: Choose objective (MLM vs ELECTRA) and masking strategy together: objective affects sample efficiency, masking affects what the model learns — both should be aligned to the target downstream tasks.  
- Integration: For constrained compute, ELECTRA-style pretraining + dynamic/span masking is a practical recipe to improve span performance faster than naive MLM training.

## Reflection
- What was the most important thing you learned in this module?  
- Which gap area do you feel least confident about? What would help you strengthen it?  
- How does Encoder-Only Pretraining connect to other topics you have studied?

## Further Reading
- [ELECTRA: Pre-training Text Encoders as Discriminators Rather Than Generators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.10555) (Research Paper) (Advanced) — Explains the replaced-token-detection objective and the generator/discriminator pretraining setup.  
- [SpanBERT: Improving Pre-training by Representing and Predicting Spans](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.10529) (Research Paper) (Advanced) — Details span masking and span-boundary objectives to improve span representations.  
- [RoBERTa: A Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.11692) (Research Paper) (Intermediate) — Discusses pretraining recipe improvements such as longer training and masking practices.  
- [The Pile: An 800GB Dataset of Diverse Text for Language Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.00027) (Research Paper) (Intermediate) — Covers data curation and dataset construction considerations relevant to pretraining corpora.  
- [LAMB: Layer-wise Adaptive Moments optimizer for Batch training](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.00962) (Research Paper) (Advanced) — Presents an optimizer useful for large-batch pretraining workflows.

MLM Masking Protocol.module_md:
## Module Overview
Imagine you are building a bidirectional encoder (like BERT) to pretrain on a large corpus, but you must decide which tokens to hide so the model learns useful bidirectional representations. The MLM Masking Protocol (the 80/10/10 rule applied to ~15% of subword tokens) is the canonical solution taught in your coursework for this problem: it creates prediction targets by masking some tokens and training the model to recover them. This topic matters now in industry because masking choices interact with model scale, compute efficiency, and downstream transfer; practitioners must both implement masking correctly at scale and tune or adapt masking strategies beyond the textbook defaults. In this module you will learn practical, industry-relevant extensions: dynamic (on-the-fly) masking, efficient mask sampling and label construction for large-scale training, and instrumentation needed to evaluate masking choices. Ready to move from “what BERT taught me” to “how I would build and evaluate masking for a production pretraining run”?

## Learning Objectives
1. Explain the standard BERT masking protocol (15% selection and 80/10/10 replacement) and why masked tokens are predicted during pretraining but not seen at fine-tuning. (Curriculum)
2. Describe the role of masked tokens in building bidirectional encoder representations and how the masking objective is framed as a prediction task. (Curriculum)
3. Design and implement a dynamic (on-the-fly) masking pipeline that samples mask positions per batch while preserving tokenization boundaries. (Gap — Apply)
4. Evaluate the effects of different masking hyperparameters (mask rate, span length, whole-word masking) on pretraining signals and downstream metrics using controlled ablations and monitoring. (Gap — Analyze)
5. Instrument a large-scale masking implementation for correctness and observability: construct labels with ignore-index handling, implement vectorized mask sampling, and monitor masked-token coverage and per-token loss. (Gap — Evaluate)

## Curriculum Coverage
The course material introduces BERT’s Masked Language Model (MLM) pretraining objective. The curriculum specifies that during pretraining, approximately 15% of (sub)word tokens are selected as prediction targets. For each selected token, the input is replaced with the special [MASK] token 80% of the time, a random token 10% of the time, and left unchanged 10% of the time; in all cases the model is trained to predict the original token. The curriculum also notes that masks are not present at fine-tuning time, so the masked tokens are a pretraining-only construct.

The treatment in the course focuses on the conceptual protocol—how many tokens to select and the 80/10/10 replacement rule—and situates MLM within bidirectional Transformer encoders. The materials briefly connect MLM to other pretraining design choices (e.g., next-sentence prediction) and contrast encoder versus decoder pretraining objectives, but the curriculum does not dive into large-scale engineering for masking, variations such as span or whole-word masking, nor into instrumentation and empirical tuning at industry scale.

Before continuing, make sure you can answer:
- What percentage of tokens does BERT select as prediction targets during MLM pretraining?
- For a selected token, what are the three replacement choices and their relative probabilities?
- Are [MASK] tokens present during fine-tuning?

## Identified Gaps
The curriculum gives a clear specification of the canonical 80/10/10 masking protocol, but industry practice demands additional skills and knowledge that the course only partially covers. These gaps are opportunities to gain practical, employable skills.

- Dynamic (on-the-fly) vs. static masking: The curriculum omits discussion of per-epoch or per-batch randomization of mask positions. This matters because dynamic masking is commonly used in industry to increase data diversity and reduce overfitting—skills critical for production-scale pretraining. Priority: (Critical).
- Engineering and instrumentation for large-scale masking: The course does not cover efficient, vectorized mask sampling, label construction with ignore-index handling, or monitoring masked-token coverage and per-token loss. These are essential for scaling pretraining pipelines and debugging runs. Priority: (Critical).
- Span and whole-word masking, alternative MLM-family objectives, and masking hyperparameter tuning: These are not covered in depth but are important for tasks that require span-level representations or for improving sample/compute efficiency. Priority: (Important).

Addressing these gaps will improve practical competence and employability in NLP engineering and research roles working on pretraining.

## Core Content

### What You Need to Learn

Gap focus 1 — Dynamic (on-the-fly) masking
- Anchor: Building on the curriculum’s 15% selection and the 80/10/10 replacement rule, dynamic masking changes *when* and *which* tokens are selected across training passes.
- Definition: Dynamic (on-the-fly) masking means sampling the subset of tokens to be predicted at batch construction time (or per epoch), rather than precomputing and reusing a single masked copy of the dataset. Each training pass can present different masked positions for the same underlying text.
- How it works (walkthrough):
  1. Given a tokenized input sequence, sample mask candidate positions at the desired overall mask rate (e.g., 15% of tokens), respecting tokenization boundaries if using whole-word masking.
  2. For the sampled positions, apply the 80/10/10 replacement rule: with 80% probability replace by [MASK], with 10% by a random token, and with 10% leave unchanged. Construct a label array where only masked positions have the original token id, and non-masked positions are set to an ignore-index for loss computation.
  3. Repeat sampling per batch, so the same sentence will typically have different masked positions on different iterations.
- Step-by-step application:
  1. Tokenize text into subword tokens and, if needed, map subword pieces to whole words for WWM (whole-word masking).
  2. For each sequence in a batch, sample k indices uniformly (or according to a span distribution) to reach the target mask rate. Use vectorized random sampling across the batch for speed.
  3. Apply replacement choices for the sampled indices, build the input batch and the label batch (labels use ignore-index for non-predicted tokens), and feed both into the encoder and loss function.
- Industry example: RoBERTa and other practical pretraining efforts use dynamic masking rather than static masked datasets; Hugging Face’s DataCollatorForLanguageModeling demonstrates an on-the-fly masking pattern for training pipelines. Dynamic masking increases diversity of prediction targets across epochs and is a common production practice.

Gap focus 2 — Engineering and instrumentation for large-scale masking
- Anchor: Building on the curriculum’s emphasis that masked tokens are predicted during pretraining, engineering resources are needed to make masking correct and observable at scale.
- Definition: Engineering and instrumentation for masking refers to efficient, correct implementation of masking (vectorized sampling, tokenization-aware masking, label construction with ignore indices) plus monitoring (masked-token coverage, per-token loss, distribution of replacement types) so masking choices can be debugged and tuned.
- How it works (walkthrough):
  1. Vectorized mask sampling: Represent sequences as batched token id tensors and sample mask selection masks using vectorized random draws (e.g., generate uniform random matrix and threshold to get ~15% positions). Use masking masks to index and modify tensors without Python loops.
  2. Tokenization-aware masking: If you use whole-word masking or span masking, precompute mappings from token positions to word spans and sample contiguous spans or whole-word groups rather than independent subword indices.
  3. Label construction and loss handling: Create a label tensor equal to original token ids where mask is True, and fill non-masked positions with a designated ignore_index understood by the loss function so only masked positions contribute to loss.
  4. Observability: Log metrics such as fraction of tokens masked per batch, counts of [MASK] vs random vs unchanged replacements, per-token or per-position loss for masked tokens, and downstream validation curves for different masking choices.
- Step-by-step application:
  1. Implement a data-collator or batch preprocessor that performs vectorized sampling and replacement given a batch of token ids.
  2. Ensure mapping from original tokens to labels uses ignore-index for non-masked tokens and that the loss function is configured accordingly.
  3. Add monitoring hooks: per-batch masked-token coverage, histogram of masked positions, and aggregated masked-token loss. Use these to detect bugs (e.g., masking special tokens) and to compare masking variants.
- Industry example: Large pretraining runs commonly instrument masked-token coverage and per-token loss to validate correct masking and to compare masking hyperparameters; RoBERTa’s pretraining choices and Hugging Face tooling exemplify how on-the-fly masking and instrumentation are used in practice.

Brief summaries of other gaps
- Span and Whole-Word Masking: Mask contiguous token spans or entire whole words to improve span-level representations; important for tasks like QA and coreference. Learn more in resources on SpanBERT and span-corruption methods.
- Alternative MLM objectives (ELECTRA, T5 span corruption): These objectives address the [MASK] mismatch and sample efficiency; industry chooses them when computation or transfer efficiency matters.
- Masking hyperparameter tuning: 15% is a heuristic; studies show optimal rates can vary by model scale and domain—run controlled ablations to find suitable mask rates.

### Common Misconceptions
- Misconception: “15% mask rate is always optimal.”  
  Why it’s wrong: Recent empirical work indicates 15% is a heuristic and not universally optimal; optimal mask rates can depend on model size and masking strategy.  
  Correct understanding: Treat 15% as a reasonable default but run controlled experiments (or consult literature) to tune mask rates for your setting.

- Misconception: “Static precomputed masking and dynamic masking are equivalent.”  
  Why it’s wrong: Static masking reuses the same masked positions each epoch, reducing diversity of prediction targets.  
  Correct understanding: Dynamic (on-the-fly) masking randomizes masked positions across epochs, increasing data diversity and helping generalization in practice.

- Misconception: “Masked tokens must appear during fine-tuning for the model to work.”  
  Why it’s wrong: The curriculum explicitly states no masks are seen at fine-tuning time; masking is a pretraining-only mechanism.  
  Correct understanding: Pretraining uses masked tokens as targets; fine-tuning uses the model representations without [MASK] tokens.

## Industry Context
Roles that value these skills include: NLP/ML Engineers working on pretraining pipelines, Research Scientists designing pretraining objectives and ablations, and Data Engineers who implement large-scale data preprocessing and batching for model training. These roles require both conceptual understanding of MLM and practical skills to implement and monitor masking at scale.

Real-world use case (example): A team training a BERT-style encoder on a multi-billion-token corpus must implement masking that (a) scales efficiently across GPUs, (b) respects tokenization boundaries for whole-word masking when needed, and (c) provides observability so masking bugs or skewed coverage can be detected. The solution uses on-the-fly (dynamic) masking implemented in a vectorized data collator, constructs labels with ignore-index so loss only aggregates masked positions, and logs masked-token coverage and per-token loss. This pipeline enables safer hyperparameter sweeps (mask rates, span lengths) and more reliable downstream transfer results—an approach reflected in industrial pretraining papers and tooling.

Employers hiring for these roles look for demonstrable experience in: implementing token-level data transforms in batch pipelines, handling tokenization-aware masking, setting up correct loss-label pipelines (ignore-index), instrumenting training for per-token and per-batch debugging, and running controlled experiments to justify masking choices.

## Practice & Review

### Quick Check
1. What fraction of tokens does BERT select as prediction targets in the curriculum’s MLM protocol?  
> Answer: 15%.

2. For a selected token under the 80/10/10 rule, what are the three replacement choices and their probabilities?  
> Answer: Replace with [MASK] 80% of the time, replace with a random token 10% of the time, leave unchanged 10% of the time.

3. Conceptual: Why is dynamic (on-the-fly) masking used in industry instead of static precomputed masking?  
> Answer: Dynamic masking randomizes mask positions per epoch or batch, increasing data diversity and reducing overfitting; it is commonly used in practice to improve pretraining efficiency and generalization.

4. Application: If you must implement MLM masking for a multi-GPU pretraining run, what high-level steps connect the curriculum’s 80/10/10 protocol to a production-ready masking pipeline?  
> Answer: Vectorize sampling of mask positions per batch to reach the target mask rate, apply 80/10/10 replacements, construct label tensor using ignore-index for non-masked tokens, feed inputs and labels to the model and loss function, and log masked-token coverage and masked-position loss for observability.

### Apply It
Scenario: You are preparing to pretrain a BERT-style encoder on a domain-specific corpus (medical notes). The baseline curriculum masking (15% selection and 80/10/10 replacements) exists, but clinicians care about span-level accuracy for entity extraction, and your compute budget is constrained. You must implement masking, instrument the pretraining run, and run at least one controlled ablation comparing static versus dynamic masking and one mask-rate variant.

Tasks:
1. Implement an on-the-fly masking data collator that applies the 80/10/10 rule and supports whole-word masking for tokenization boundaries.  
2. Construct labels using an ignore-index so only masked positions contribute to MLM loss.  
3. Add instrumentation: per-batch masked-token coverage, histogram of masked positions, counts of replacement types, and per-masked-token loss.  
4. Run two short pretraining experiments (static masking vs dynamic masking) and a third experiment with a different mask rate; produce a brief report comparing masked-token loss curves and downstream entity extraction validation scores.

Expected deliverable: A data-collator implementation (or pseudocode), logs and plots of masking metrics and masked-token losses, and a short ablation report with recommendations on masking strategy and mask rate for the medical corpus.

## Key Takeaways
- Curriculum: The BERT MLM protocol selects ~15% of subword tokens as prediction targets and uses the 80/10/10 replacement rule (80% [MASK], 10% random token, 10% unchanged).  
- Curriculum: Masked tokens are pretraining-only targets; models are not exposed to [MASK] tokens during fine-tuning.  
- Curriculum: MLM enables bidirectional encoder pretraining by creating supervised prediction targets within otherwise unsupervised text.

- Gap: Dynamic (on-the-fly) masking randomizes masked positions per batch/epoch, increasing data diversity and is widely used in industry.  
- Gap: Engineering correctly at scale requires vectorized mask sampling, tokenization-aware masking (for whole-word or span masking), label construction with ignore-index, and monitoring of mask coverage and per-token loss.  
- Gap: 15% is a heuristic — mask rate, span distributions, and whole-word vs. subword masking should be empirically tuned for model size and domain.  
- Gap: Alternative MLM-family objectives (e.g., replaced-token detection, span corruption) exist to address the [MASK] mismatch and sample efficiency; industry selects them based on compute and transfer tradeoffs.

- Integration: To move from coursework to deployable pretraining, combine the curriculum’s 80/10/10 protocol with dynamic masking and robust engineering/instrumentation to ensure correctness and to enable empirical tuning.  
- Integration: Controlled ablations and observed masked-token metrics are the practical bridge between theoretical masking choices and downstream performance.

## Reflection

- Which gap area do you feel least confident about? What would help you strengthen it?
- How does MLM Masking Protocol connect to other topics you have studied?

## Further Reading
- [RoBERTa: A Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.11692) (Research Paper) (Advanced) — Discusses practical pretraining choices and includes notes on dynamic masking and engineering decisions used in robust pretraining.  
- [DataCollatorForLanguageModeling — Hugging Face Transformers Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main_classes/data_collator#data-collator-for-language-modeling) (Documentation) (Intermediate) — Shows an on-the-fly masking implementation pattern useful for building a production data collator.

Span Masking in SpanBERT.module_md:
## Module Overview
Imagine you are building an extractive question-answering system over internal documents and find your model often fails to correctly score or extract multi-word answers (spans) even though it recognizes individual words. Span masking in SpanBERT targets this exact failure mode by training encoders to learn stronger representations for contiguous spans rather than isolated subword tokens. Right now industry values span-aware pretraining because many production tasks (QA, NER, coreference resolution, text infilling) rely on robust multi-token span representations.

In this short module you will move beyond classroom descriptions of contiguous-span masking and gain practical skills: how to sample and mask spans (dynamic masking, span-length distributions, whole-word handling), how to implement efficient data-collators for pretraining, and how to construct and train span-boundary prediction heads used in SpanBERT-style objectives. By the end you will be able to design and prototype a span-masking pretraining pipeline suitable for downstream span tasks.

Ready to close the gap between conceptual understanding and industry-ready implementation?

## Learning Objectives
1. Explain the motivation for contiguous span-level masking and the span-boundary representation idea (Curriculum).
2. Describe the differences between token-level MLM and span-level masking, including dynamic masking and whole-word considerations (Curriculum).
3. Implement a data-collator that performs dynamic contiguous-span sampling and masking for a mini pretraining run (Gap).
4. Construct span-boundary representations from encoder hidden states and implement a prediction head to train on span targets (Gap).
5. Evaluate and compare the impact of different span-length sampling distributions (e.g., geometric vs. fixed n-grams) on a downstream QA fine-tuning metric and recommend hyperparameters based on observed trade-offs (Gap).

## Curriculum Coverage
The course introduces SpanBERT as an extension of BERT-style masked language modeling that focuses on contiguous span masking rather than masking isolated (sub)word tokens. It contrasts BERT’s token-level masked LM (predicting random 15% of subword tokens with an 80/10/10 replacement schedule) with SpanBERT’s approach of masking contiguous spans to create a harder pretraining task. The curriculum emphasizes that span-level masking helps models learn representations useful for span-centric tasks like NER, coreference, and question answering.

The materials also cover the concept of span-boundary representations — a span-centric target that encourages the encoder to summarize span content compactly — and note that SpanBERT and related variants are part of a family of BERT extensions (alongside RoBERTa) that obtain gains mainly by changing masking/objective and scaling pretraining. Treatment in the course is conceptual and focused on motivations, definitions, and high-level techniques rather than low-level implementation details or production engineering patterns.

Before continuing, make sure you can answer:
- What is the primary difference between BERT’s MLM and SpanBERT’s masking strategy?
- Why are span-boundary representations introduced in SpanBERT?
- What downstream tasks are most likely to benefit from span-level pretraining?

## Identified Gaps
The curriculum gives a clear conceptual picture but leaves several practical, high-value industry skills underdeveloped — each is an opportunity to build employable expertise.

- Missing hands-on implementation guidance for span sampling and masking: industry expects you to implement dynamic masking, choose span-length sampling distributions (e.g., geometric), and handle overlapping spans and subword/whole-word boundaries. This matters because the sampling strategy materially affects what the model learns and how it transfers to tasks like QA and coreference. Priority: (Critical).

- Lack of engineering details for efficient data pipelines: constructing data-collators that produce masked inputs and corresponding targets, batching strategies for variable-length masked spans, and GPU-memory tradeoffs are often required in production pretraining. This is directly tied to the ability to prototype and scale a SpanBERT-style objective. Priority: (Critical).

- Underdeveloped description of span-boundary representation mechanics: the curriculum names span-boundary representations as important but does not teach how to compute boundary vectors, parameterize the prediction head, or set up the loss. Industry hiring expects you to implement and tune such heads. Priority: (Important).

- Fewer practical evaluation recipes and hyperparameter starting points: industry practitioners expect evaluation protocols for span-centric tasks and sensible hyperparameter baselines. Priority: (Important).

Each of these gaps is a practical skill you can add to make your pretraining experiments reproducible and useful for real-world span tasks.

## Core Content

### What You Need to Learn
We target the two highest-priority gaps: (1) span sampling & masking implementation, and (2) span-boundary representation construction and training. Building on your curriculum knowledge of MLM and the idea of contiguous-span masking, below are concrete, actionable recipes you can implement.

Gap 1 — Span sampling and dynamic masking (critical)
- Definition and anchor: Building on BERT’s MLM and the curriculum’s explanation of contiguous-span masking, span sampling is the procedure that decides which contiguous sequences of tokens to mask, their lengths, and how often masking is refreshed during training (dynamic vs static).
- How it works (walkthrough and rationale):
  - Dynamic masking: masks are resampled each epoch/step so the model sees different missing spans over time; this prevents overfitting to a fixed mask pattern and encourages generalization.
  - Span-length distribution: rather than choosing fixed n-grams, practitioners often sample span lengths from a geometric or other skewed distribution so short spans occur more frequently but longer spans still appear occasionally, matching natural span statistics.
  - Whole-word and subword handling: ensure spans respect word boundaries when whole-word masking is desired; with subword tokenization, either expand the span to include all subword pieces of a word or perform masking at token-piece level depending on objective.
- Application steps (implementing a simple dynamic span masker):
  1. Tokenize a raw text example into token IDs (subword tokens).
  2. Decide the total proportion of tokens to mask per example (e.g., target_masked_fraction parameter).
  3. While the number of masked tokens < target:
     a. Sample a span length L from a span-length distribution (e.g., geometric with parameter p, or a preset n-gram sampler).
     b. Sample a start index uniformly from the set of allowed start positions.
     c. If whole-word masking is enabled, expand the span to cover full words (group subword pieces).
     d. If the chosen span would overlap an already-masked token, either skip (non-overlapping) or merge/allow overlap per your policy.
     e. Mark the span tokens as masked.
  4. Apply replacement policy (analogous to BERT’s 80/10/10) for masked tokens or for SpanBERT you may replace the entire span with mask tokens (or per your model’s expected input format).
  5. Produce target labels that include all masked token IDs (or an aggregated span target if using a boundary objective).
- Practical example from industry practice:
  - A common industry pattern is to implement dynamic masking inside a DataCollator that operates at batch-creation time so each epoch sees new masks. For span-length sampling, practitioners often use a geometric-like sampler so that L=1 is common but L>1 also occurs — this yields a more varied pretraining signal that benefits downstream span tasks.

Gap 2 — Span-boundary representations and prediction heads (critical)
- Definition and anchor: Building on the curriculum’s statement that SpanBERT uses span-boundary representations to improve span-level modeling, a span-boundary representation is a compact vector summary derived from encoder hidden states at the span’s boundaries (and optionally pooled interior information) used as the target or input to a prediction head.
- How it works (walkthrough and rationale):
  - Why boundaries: using boundary token vectors forces the encoder to store summary information about the internal tokens in the surrounding hidden states, producing compact span embeddings without requiring a separate decoder to reconstruct full tokens.
  - Common constructions: compute the boundary representation by concatenating the encoder hidden vector for the first token and the last token of the span, optionally adding elementwise difference or a learned projection. Pass this combined vector through a small feed-forward network (prediction head) to produce predictions — e.g., to predict masked interior tokens, to classify span types, or to produce span embeddings for downstream tasks.
- Application steps (implementing a span-boundary head):
  1. Run your masked input through the Transformer encoder to obtain hidden states H (sequence length × hidden_dim).
  2. For each masked span (start s, end e):
     a. Extract h_s (hidden vector at start token) and h_e (hidden vector at end token).
     b. Form a boundary vector b = [h_s; h_e] (concatenation) or b = W_cat([h_s; h_e]) (projected).
  3. Pass b through a feed-forward prediction head: y_pred = FFN(b) where FFN is a small MLP with nonlinearity and output dimension compatible with the target (classification logits, span embedding, or token reconstruction).
  4. Define loss: for boundary-prediction objectives you might supervise y_pred to predict properties of the masked span (e.g., classification labels or a target embedding); in SpanBERT’s design the boundary head is trained to help the encoder represent the span compactly (see the original SpanBERT paper for exact loss formulations).
  5. Backpropagate and update encoder + head jointly.
- Practical example from industry practice:
  - An industry practitioner converting a BERT checkpoint to SpanBERT-style pretraining will add a small MLP to the encoder that takes concatenated boundary vectors and outputs either token prediction logits or a span-level embedding; they train this head jointly with dynamic span masking so that boundary vectors encode the span semantics needed for QA and coreference tasks.

Brief summaries of remaining lesser gaps (where to learn more):
- Data-collator efficiency and batching: what it is — code patterns for creating masked batches on the fly; why it matters — memory and throughput tradeoffs; where to learn more — HuggingFace examples (see Further Reading).
- Evaluation recipes & hyperparameters: what it is — protocols for SQuAD/NER fine-tuning and metrics; why it matters — measuring real transfer; where to learn more — SpanBERT paper and SQuAD explorer.

### Common Misconceptions
- Misconception: "Span masking is just masking multiple adjacent tokens, so implementation is trivial and identical to token-level MLM."  
  Why it’s wrong: span masking involves decisions about span-length distribution, whole-word vs. subword expansion, overlap policies, and whether masking is dynamic — all of which affect learning signals.  
  Correct understanding: implementors must design sampling and replacement policies and typically use dynamic masking and whole-word handling to get the intended benefits.

- Misconception: "Span-boundary representations always require reconstructing every masked token inside the span."  
  Why it’s wrong: boundary-based objectives aim to teach the encoder to encode span content compactly via boundary vectors and a prediction head; they do not necessarily require a full autoregressive reconstruction decoder.  
  Correct understanding: boundary prediction heads can be designed to predict token IDs, span classes, or embeddings — different choices affect computational cost and the kinds of downstream gains.

- Misconception: "Static masking (one fixed mask per example) is adequate for span pretraining."  
  Why it’s wrong: static masks limit the variety of masked contexts the model sees, which can reduce generalization to unseen spans.  
  Correct understanding: dynamic masking (reshuffling masks across epochs) is commonly used in industry to present more varied learning signals.

## Industry Context
Roles that value span-masking and span-boundary expertise:
- NLP Research Scientist working on pretraining objectives and model architectures.
- Machine Learning Engineer (NLP) responsible for pretraining or adapting language models for production QA/NER systems.
- Applied NLP Engineer specializing in information extraction, coreference resolution, or retrieval-augmented QA.

Real-world use case (detailed): A company building an enterprise document QA product struggles to accurately extract multi-word answers from long documents. They pretrain a Transformer encoder with a SpanBERT-style objective: dynamic contiguous-span masking and a span-boundary prediction head. During fine-tuning on an extractive QA dataset, the span-aware encoder yields higher span-F1 and exact-match scores, particularly on answers that are multi-token entities. The outcome: fewer failed extractions, improved user satisfaction, and reduced need for rule-based post-processing.

Skills employers look for:
- Ability to design and implement dynamic span masking and whole-word handling in data pipelines.
- Experience adding and training span-boundary heads on top of Transformer encoders.
- Practical evaluation knowledge: fine-tuning on span extraction benchmarks (e.g., SQuAD) and interpreting span-centric metrics.

## Practice & Review

### Quick Check
1. What does SpanBERT change about the standard BERT masked LM objective?  
> Answer: It masks contiguous spans of tokens (span-level masking) rather than isolated (sub)word tokens to create a harder pretraining task focused on spans.  

2. Name one downstream task that benefits from span-level pretraining.  
> Answer: Extractive question answering (QA); also NER and coreference resolution.  

3. Conceptual: Why is dynamic masking preferred over static masking in span-level pretraining?  
> Answer: Dynamic masking reshuffles masks each epoch so models see varied masked contexts, improving generalization and preventing overfit to fixed mask patterns.  

4. Application: When constructing a boundary representation for a span, what encoder states do you use and how might you turn them into a prediction?  
> Answer: Use the encoder hidden vectors at the span’s start and end tokens; concatenate (or otherwise combine) them and feed into a small feed-forward network as a prediction head for span targets.

### Apply It
Scenario: Your team must prototype a small pretraining run to test whether span-level masking improves extraction quality for your internal QA dataset. You have a BERT-base checkpoint, a tokenizer that produces subword pieces, and a GPU single-node training setup. You need to produce masked batches on the fly, add a span-boundary prediction head, and run a few epochs of pretraining before fine-tuning on your QA data.

Tasks:
- Implement a DataCollator that performs dynamic contiguous-span sampling with a configurable span-length sampler and whole-word masking option.
- Add a span-boundary prediction head to the encoder that takes concatenated boundary hidden states and outputs a target-compatible prediction, and integrate its loss with the MLM loss.
- Run a mini pretraining experiment (few epochs) and then fine-tune the checkpoint on your QA dev set to compare span-F1 and exact-match to the baseline.

Expected outcome/deliverable:
- A reproducible mini-experiment repository including the data-collator code, model modifications, a short training script, and a short report showing QA dev metrics comparing baseline and span-pretrained models.

## Key Takeaways
- Curriculum: SpanBERT extends BERT-style MLM by masking contiguous spans rather than isolated (sub)word tokens to strengthen span representations.
- Curriculum: The course introduces span-boundary representations as a span-centric target that encourages compact span embeddings useful for tasks like QA, NER, and coreference.
- Curriculum: The treatment in the course is conceptual and explains motivations and high-level differences from BERT/ RoBERTa without deep implementation detail.
- Gap: (Gap) Dynamic masking and careful span-length sampling are critical implementation choices; industry practitioners resample masks and use skewed (e.g., geometric-like) span-length distributions to produce varied signals.
- Gap: (Gap) Building an efficient data-collator that creates masked batches on the fly and respects whole-word/subword tokenization is a high-impact engineering skill for pretraining.
- Gap: (Gap) Span-boundary representations are typically built from encoder boundary hidden states passed through a small prediction head; you should know how to construct and supervise this head.
- Gap: (Gap) Evaluating span pretraining requires fine-tuning on span-centric tasks (SQuAD, NER) and checking span-level metrics (exact match, F1).
- Integration: (Integration) Combining curriculum knowledge of why span masking helps with practical skills (sampling, data-collation, head design) enables you to prototype SpanBERT-style pretraining that industry can adopt.
- Integration: (Integration) The most practical experiments integrate dynamic masking in the data pipeline and joint training of boundary heads with the encoder to observe improvements on downstream span tasks.

## Reflection
- What was the most important thing you learned in this module?
- Which gap area do you feel least confident about? What would help you strengthen it?
- How does Span Masking in SpanBERT connect to other topics you have studied?

## Further Reading
